source.title: Interpreting Latent Protein Language Model Features with Geometric Annotations
source.authors: S. Setlur; Djordje Mihajlovic; Darrick Lee

record.tranche_reason: Applies sparse-autoencoder analysis to protein language models, a new model setting, and reports results about recoverable and interpretable sparse features. It does not test toy-model superposition or feature competition directly.
record.gate_note: The paper trains SAEs on ESM-2 representations and reports reconstruction, sparsity, and geometric predictability of SAE activations; these bear on V4 as indirect evidence in a protein language model. It does not vary feature sparsity or importance, measure overlap or orthogonality of feature directions, or test capacity competition. Its contact-map ablations are recorded separately but do not directly measure a listed version. Results comparing database, motif, and position annotations are not included as claim-version rows.
record.test_reason: The paper uses ReLU SAEs on ESM-2 as a tool and reports the performance of its own geometric annotation pipeline against InterPro, motif and position baselines. It never asks whether ESM-2 superposes features, whether neurons are polysemantic, or whether SAE features are the model's units. Table 6 reconstruction and ℓ0 figures are appendix training details for SAEs chosen by best loss recovered, not a test of V4. At layer 6 the mean ℓ0 (726.5) exceeds the 320-dim input, so near-total loss recovery there says little about recovering sparse features. No neuron-basis comparison is made. Annotation coverage (Tables 1, 2, 9, 10) measures how well geometry predicts SAE activations. That is a related construct, recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially right. The authors conclude that geometric annotation expands coverage of ESM-2 8M SAE features beyond database and sequence methods. They also conclude it splits shared InterPro labels into finer geometric motifs and transfers to some metagenomic proteins: only 1.7–4.1% of features have median PR-AUC >0.5 there. Finally, they find these features are coupled to contact-map predictions under ablation, described as preliminary contact-level interventions.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains ReLU SAEs on ESM-2 protein-language-model residual streams and evaluates feature annotations and contact-map ablations; it does not reproduce the original toy-network superposition experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Geometric annotation predictive strength varies by layer and model: the held-out PR-AUC distributions differ across ESM-2 8M layers and ESM-2 35M layer 6.

fits_no_version.finding: Local Cα-backbone geometry predicts residue-level activation of 84–94% of ESM-2 8M SAE features above a shuffle null (q<0.05), and 93% for 35M layer 6. Most features have low held-out PR-AUC, though: 82–95% are below 0.3 in 8M and 63% in 35M.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features in protein language models are significantly, but mostly weakly, predictable from local backbone geometry.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating geometry-annotated SAE features at ESM-2 8M layer 4 shifts predicted contact maps toward the target descriptor. For the top 200 features, 122/200 shift more than matched controls.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some geometry-annotated pLM SAE features are causally coupled to contact predictions.

record.problems: The authors note that the main analysis uses predicted structures and is limited to ESM-2 8M for contact-map interventions; contact-level interventions do not validate full folding behavior. They also state that the fixed-score permutation test does not account for model fitting, that the BH procedure does not provide simultaneous validation of aggregate results, and that metagenomic structure predictions are less robust. For many geometrically annotated features, held-out PR-AUC is low.
record.rows_left_out: Annotation results for InterPro protein/residue labels, sequence motifs, and positional predicates are omitted because they do not directly test a listed claim version. Other SAE metrics in Table 6, including reconstruction loss, sparsity loss, total loss, and dead-feature counts, are omitted because the reported loss-recovery, variance-independent sparsity, and annotation results already capture the relevant dictionary recovery evidence.

untested.parts: No toy models; no variation of sparsity or importance; no measure of feature overlap, orthogonality or geometry of decoder directions.
No test of capacity competition or of dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Neuron polysemanticity is not measured; it is only cited as motivation.
There is no neuron-basis analysis and no baseline for SAE fidelity or sparsity. SAE metrics are selected-run training details, with ℓ0 at or above the input dimension.
No test of completeness, stability across seeds or sizes, or canonicality of SAE features. Dictionary size was a sweep variable but results are reported only for the selected 32× SAEs.
No analysis of multi-dimensional versus 1-D features.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T3/tests framing rests on SAE training metrics and annotation coverage. Neither addresses superposition. The paper cites Toy Models only as background on polysemanticity. Dead features at layer 2 (533–580 of 10,240) and variance explained (0.92–0.96) are also in Table 6, but they share the same selection caveat. The rows and source are left as they are for researchers to judge.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, excess sparse features, overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity results from capacity pressure or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemanticity can arise without capacity pressure.
The study concerns protein language models, not a range of general-purpose LLMs; it does not establish feature spreading across neurons in LLMs generally.
Completeness, stability, or canonicality of SAE features.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The SAEs have high reported loss recovery and sparse activations, and geometric predictors significantly annotate large fractions of features; held-out PR-AUC results show stronger prediction for some features. Rows R1–R14.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Most geometrically annotated features are in the 0.0–0.3 PR-AUC band for ESM-2 8M layers 2, 4, and 6, so significant annotation does not imply strong predictive strength for most features. Rows R11–R13.
